newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian PM invites Congress Party to help on budget.
newsitem.headline: Indian PM invites Congress Party to help on budget.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Wednesday invited the Congress Party, which gives his government make-or-break support, to help frame the next budget.
The Press Trust of India said Deve Gowda warned political parties against wooing voters with populist promises saying "unhealthy competition" among rival groups could result in economic bankruptcy.

The news agency quoted Deve Gowda as telling reporters on board his special plane that the Congress Party, which supports his 13-party coalition in parliament, could set up a sub-committee to coordinate its views with the government.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is due to present the 1997/98 (April-March) budget at the end of February.
Deve Gowda's seven-month-old United Front coalition faces tough choices.
Chidambaram wants to push through measures to control the government deficit, but communist allies have warned against any move to raise state-controlled prices of petroleum or wheat.
Deve Gowda's United Front alliance has rejected any interference with the budget by rival political parties, saying budget-making is the prerogative of the prime minister and the finance minister.

PTI quoted the prime minister as saying he was prepared to take "advice" from Congress if its president, Sitaram Kesri, set up a committee of senior deputies to discuss budget proposals with the ruling alliance's policy-making Steering Committee.

Deve Gowda was quoted this week as denying any government move to increase the price of subsidised petroleum products, a sensitive political issue, after Congress and the rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata party opposed the move.
A key Deve Gowda ally was quoted on Wednesday as welcoming any move for Congress to join the government.
The Asian Age newspaper quoted communist Agriculture Minister Chaturanan Mishra as saying Congress was welcome to join if it gave up its support for disinvestment in state-owned companies.
The Congress party under former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao started sweeping economic reforms from 1991.
Lack of public support for the reforms was seen as a major reason for the party's worst-ever election defeat in last year's general elections.
